screens.title: File System Analysis — What to look for
screens.narratorSegment: File system analysis is often the first step in an investigation because it reveals persistent artifacts left on storage media. Define the scope: which file system type are you examining, NTFS or ext4, and which image represents the evidence? Start by listing directory structures and metadata to find files with unusual names, extensions, or placement. Pay attention to MAC times — modification, access, and creation timestamps — because they help sequence activity. For example, a deleted executable recovered from a temporary folder with a recent creation time but an older modification time could indicate it was copied or dropped and then executed. Use tools like Autopsy or command-line utilities to recover deleted entries if they are not yet overwritten. A common mistake is to accept a timestamp at face value without checking for time-zone shifts or system clock manipulation; corroborate with logs, registry entries, or network timestamps. Practice: run the stat command on a suspicious file to read its timestamps and compare those timestamps to related artifacts. Takeaway: file system artifacts provide durable clues, but they must be correlated with other sources to build a reliable timeline.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › File System Analysis
Definition

File system analysis inspects structure, metadata, and file contents to find evidence such as deleted files, unusual directories, and timestamp patterns.

Key checks
  • Recover deleted files and check if they are overwritten.
  • Read Modification, Access, Creation timestamps and compare.
  • Look for executables in temporary or user folders with mismatched timestamps.
  • Inspect file extensions, names that mimic system files, and hidden attributes.
Command Example
stat /path/to/suspicious_file
This command reveals MAC times used in timeline construction.
Example Scenario
An investigator recovers a deleted executable found in a temporary directory with creation time after the system reboot time. The file's modification time predates creation, suggesting it may have been copied or reconstructed on the host. The investigator searches for matching registry Run entries and memory process lists to confirm execution.
Common Mistake
Assuming timestamps are absolute without checking for time skew or deliberate clock changes; always corroborate across artifacts.
Key Takeaway
Use MAC times to build candidate events, then validate with registry, memory, and network artifacts.

screens.title: Deleted & Hidden Files — Recovery and pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Recovering deleted files can produce direct evidence of attacker tools or data, but recovery has caveats. When a file is deleted, its directory entry may be removed while the underlying data blocks remain until overwritten. Forensic tools can often reconstruct these files if the sectors are intact, but success depends on subsequent disk activity. Use reputable tools like Autopsy, FTK, or EnCase to carve files from unallocated space and check file signatures against extensions. A common pitfall is relying solely on filename or extension: attackers often rename binaries or hide payloads in uncommon extensions. Another pitfall is not documenting recovery context; record offsets, hashes, and the tool used so recovered files are traceable. Also watch for cases where file timestamps do not match typical usage patterns; cross-check with registry entries for program execution, memory process lists for live evidence, and network logs for related connections. Example: you find a carved executable whose hash matches a known malware sample; confirm whether a registry Run key or a memory process with that filename existed at the same time before concluding execution. Takeaway: recovery yields candidates; corroboration yields confidence.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Deleted & Hidden Files
How recovery works
  • Deleted directory entries are removed; data blocks may remain until overwritten.
  • Carving reconstructs files by scanning unallocated space for signatures.
  • Success depends on overwrite activity and fragmentation.
Example
A carved executable matches a malware hash. Instead of concluding execution, the investigator verifies registry Run keys and memory process lists to see if the binary was launched, avoiding a false positive based only on a match.
Comparison: Filename vs Content
Filename
Easily changed by attackers; weak indicator of identity.
Content/Hash
File signatures and hashes provide stronger matches, but still require context to prove execution.
Common Mistake
Concluding a file was executed based solely on its presence on disk. Always seek registry entries, memory evidence, or network activity that corroborates execution.

screens.title: Windows Registry Analysis — Artifacts and hives
screens.narratorSegment: The Windows Registry is a hierarchical database that records configuration and activity. As an investigator, registry hives such as NTUSER. DAT, SOFTWARE, SYSTEM, and SAM contain a wealth of forensic artifacts. For example, Run keys can reveal programs configured for startup, and UserAssist entries show programs that the user executed through the GUI. Registry entries also capture recently opened documents in RecentDocs and USB device connections that help establish device history. Tools such as RegRipper parse hives into readable outputs, pulling relevant keys into a forensic timeline. When analyzing the Registry, note that timestamps are not always explicit as file MAC times are; some entries include last-write timestamps which you should interpret carefully. A good practice is to export hive data, compute hashes for extracted artifacts, and cross-correlate with disk and memory findings. One misconception is expecting the Registry to contain only configuration — it records user behavior too. The Registry often fills gaps left by deleted files because it stores persistent metadata about actions taken on the system. Windows Registry Analysis — Artifacts and hives means registry hives record system and user actions that can reveal executed programs, persistence, and device connections not visible in file listings alone.. In practical terms, extracting evidence of execution, user activity, and device history from registry hives. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Windows Registry Analysis
Important Hives
  • NTUSER.DAT — per-user settings and RecentDocs entries.
  • SOFTWARE — installed applications and configuration.
  • SYSTEM — system configuration and device driver info.
  • SAM — account information (sensitive).
Tools
RegRipper, Registry exports parsed carefully from forensic images; avoid opening hives on live originals.
Key Artifacts and What They Mean
Run Keys
Programs configured to run at startup. Presence can indicate persistence mechanisms used by malware.
UserAssist
Tracks GUI program execution frequency and last-run information for a given user profile.
RecentDocs
Lists of recently opened files which help place user activity in time.
USB History
Device connection records that help identify data transfer vectors or evidence-bearing devices.
Example
Finding an executable in a Run key that matches a carved file and a process in a memory capture connects disk, registry, and RAM evidence to support the hypothesis that the binary ran on the host.

screens.title: Memory Forensics — Volatility commands
screens.narratorSegment: Memory forensics uncovers volatile evidence that never reaches disk, such as running processes, open network sockets, injected code, and shell histories. The Volatility Framework provides plugins to list processes, scan for sockets, and detect hidden processes. When you have a memory dump and the correct profile — for example, Win7SP1x64 for a Windows 7 SP1 64-bit image — you can run pslist to enumerate processes, netscan to show network connections, psxview to compare process lists and reveal hidden ones, and cmdscan to recover command-line histories from shells. These outputs help you identify suspicious processes such as unknown executables or those with network activity. A concrete example: using pslist shows a process named evil. exe with PID 1234; netscan shows PID 1234 connected to 192.0.2.50 on port 8080. This pairing suggests active malicious communication. Remember to record the profile used, the plugin outputs, and computed hashes for any extracted dumps so your analysis is reproducible. A common misconception is assuming memory analysis is always straightforward; differences in OS versions and the need for the correct profile can affect results and require careful validation. Takeaway: memory analysis often reveals live evidence that complements disk and registry artifacts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Memory Forensics — Volatility
Common Volatility Commands
# List running processes
vol.py -f memdump.raw --profile=Win7SP1x64 pslist

# List network connections
vol.py -f memdump.raw --profile=Win7SP1x64 netscan

# Find hidden processes
vol.py -f memdump.raw --profile=Win7SP1x64 psxview

# Extract command history from a shell
vol.py -f memdump.raw --profile=Win7SP1x64 cmdscan
Replace the profile with the correct one for the target OS; profile mismatch can produce incorrect or missing plugin output.
Example Analysis
If pslist shows evil.exe (PID 1234) and netscan shows PID 1234 connecting to 192.0.2.50:8080, that pairing indicates an active malicious process communicating externally and is a high-priority artifact to extract and document.
Pro Tip
Record the Volatility profile and plugin outputs as separate files, compute hashes of extracted data, and include them in your report for reproducibility and chain of custody.

screens.title: Volatility Walkthrough — Practical steps
screens.narratorSegment: When you approach a memory dump, follow a reproducible process. Step one is to identify the correct Volatility profile, which matches the OS version and service pack so plugins interpret structures correctly. If you know the target is Windows 7 SP1 64-bit, use Win7SP1x64. Step two is to produce a process list with pslist to get a baseline of running programs. Step three is to run netscan to find open sockets and map them to process identifiers. If a PID appears in both outputs with suspicious network activity, flag it and run psxview to look for signs of hiding techniques. Use cmdscan to recover shell command histories that might reveal attacker commands. Throughout, export plugin output to text files and compute hashes for each exported artifact. A concrete conceptual walk-through: identify the profile as Win7SP1x64, run pslist, see evil. exe PID 1234, run netscan to confirm outward connection, then extract the memory region for that PID for deeper analysis. A common misconception is skipping profile validation; it is the single most common cause of misleading results. In practical terms, a conceptual live run: identify profile, list processes, and investigate suspicious pids. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Volatility Walkthrough
Step-by-step Process
  1. Confirm the memory image and target OS; choose the Volatility profile.
  2. Run pslist to enumerate processes and note suspicious names or PIDs.
  3. Run netscan to find sockets and map them to PIDs.
  4. Run psxview to identify processes hidden from one or more views.
  5. Export outputs, extract PID memory regions, compute hashes, and document.
Conceptual Commands
vol.py -f memdump.raw --profile=Win7SP1x64 pslist
vol.py -f memdump.raw --profile=Win7SP1x64 netscan
vol.py -f memdump.raw --profile=Win7SP1x64 psxview
vol.py -f memdump.raw --profile=Win7SP1x64 cmdscan
Check Your Understanding
If pslist shows a process and netscan shows no sockets for that PID, consider whether the process used ephemeral sockets or was not networked; look for DLL injections or command history for context.

screens.title: Network Forensics — PCAP analysis with tshark
screens.narratorSegment: Network forensics analyzes captured traffic to reveal communication patterns and potential exfiltration. PCAPs contain packet-level detail that helps you answer who communicated with whom and what protocols were used. Use tshark or Wireshark to apply display filters that focus on relevant traffic. Examples include filtering HTTP requests to a suspicious host or DNS queries for a malicious domain. An investigator might run a filter for HTTP traffic to a specific IP to find suspicious uploads, or filter DNS queries for a domain under investigation. Practical checks include measuring transfer sizes and timing to detect large data transfers that suggest exfiltration. Correlate network timestamps with file system and memory timestamps to see if a file was created locally just before a large upload. A common misconception is assuming encrypted channels hide all evidence; metadata such as destination IP, timing, and session sizes remain valuable. Example commands from the source show how to filter by HTTP requests and DNS queries using tshark. Takeaway: network artifacts offer visibility into attacker communication patterns and are essential for understanding the scope of compromise. Network Forensics — PCAP analysis with tshark means pcap analysis provides destination hosts, protocol usage, and transfer characteristics that help identify exfiltration and c2 channels.. In practical terms, filtering traffic, identifying suspicious hosts, and spotting exfiltration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: PCAP analysis provides destination hosts, protocol usage, and transfer characteristics that help identify exfiltration and C2 channels.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Network Forensics — PCAPs
Filtering examples
# Filter for HTTP requests to a specific host
tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "http.request and ip.dst==192.168.1.100"

# Filter for DNS queries for a domain
tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "dns and dns.qry.name==malicious.com"
Use display filters to narrow large captures to relevant sessions and then inspect payload sizes and timestamps.
Investigative focus
  • Look for repeated connections to unusual external hosts.
  • Measure transfer sizes and timing for exfiltration indicators.
  • Correlate with file system timestamps to identify transferred files.
Misconception
Encrypted payloads conceal content but not metadata such as destination IPs, ports, and transfer volumes — those remain useful for triage.

screens.title: Correlation & Timeline Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Timeline analysis is the act of correlating timestamps and artifacts across multiple sources to build a chronological reconstruction of the incident. Start by extracting MAC times from files, last-write times from registry entries, process start times from memory captures, and packet timestamps from PCAPs. Normalize timestamps to a common reference, accounting for timezone and clock skew. Place candidate events on a timeline and look for chains of causality: a file created, a registry Run key added, a process with that filename running in memory, and a network connection soon after strongly suggests execution and external communication. Use hashes and offsets as persistent identifiers for artifacts across sources and include them in timeline entries. Beware of over-weighting a single artifact; prefer patterns and corroborated sequences. A practical example: a carved binary's creation time aligns with a Run key last-write time and a netscan connection to an external IP; that cluster forms a high-confidence event. The takeaway: timelines turn isolated artifacts into a narrative that answers what, when, and how. Correlation & Timeline Analysis means normalization and correlation of artifacts across sources create a defensible timeline that supports investigative conclusions.. In practical terms, synthesizing disk, registry, memory, and network artifacts into an event timeline. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Forensic Report — Structure and focus
screens.narratorSegment: The forensic report is the final product of the analysis and must communicate findings clearly and objectively. Begin with an executive summary that answers the critical questions in plain language: what happened, when, how, and who was involved as far as evidence shows. Follow with case details and scope: which drives, memory dumps, and PCAPs were examined. Document tools and methodology so others can reproduce the work, and include hashes and export filenames. Findings should be organized by artifact type — file system findings, registry findings, memory findings, and network findings — and each finding should include description, artifact location, significance, timestamps, and identifiers such as hashes. Provide a timeline of events reconstructed from correlated artifacts, then offer conclusions that explicitly address the investigative questions. Finish with actionable recommendations to mitigate future risk and append raw exports, logs, and chain-of-custody forms. Avoid overly technical language in the executive summary, but include technical detail in appendices for legal review. A common mistake is burying key conclusions in technical minutiae; place the answer up front and the evidence behind it. Forensic Report — Structure and focus means a good report answers the core questions up front, documents methods and evidence, and separates executive conclusions from technical appendices.. In practical terms, transforming technical artifacts into a clear report for technical and non-technical audiences. Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Forensic Report
Suggested Report Sections
  • Executive Summary — concise answers to the investigative questions.
  • Case Details and Scope — which artefacts and images were examined.
  • Tools and Methodologies — list tools and versions used during analysis.
  • Findings — organized by file system, registry, memory, and network with descriptions and significance.
  • Timeline of Events — correlated chronology with confidence levels.
  • Conclusions and Recommendations — clear, actionable steps.
  • Appendices — raw logs, hashes, and chain-of-custody forms.
Example finding entry
Description: Suspicious executable 'evil.exe' recovered from unallocated space. Location: offset 0x1A2B3C. Significance: Matches network connection and registry Run key. Timestamp: creation 2021-05-01T10:12:00Z. Hash: SHA256: <compute and list hash>.
Reporting Tip
Put the executive summary first and append technical exports. This helps managers and legal reviewers get the answer quickly while preserving detail for forensic review.

screens.title: Safe Practices & Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Safe and defensible forensic practice begins with preserving the original evidence and working only on verified copies. Create forensic images with hashing to prove integrity, and never run analysis tools against live originals to avoid accidental modification. Maintain an isolated analysis workstation to reduce the risk of network contamination and document every action in a lab log. Common mistakes include making assumptions based on one artifact, failing to document tool versions and parameters, and forgetting to collect hashes for exported artifacts. Another frequent error is not correlating artifacts across sources, which can lead to false attribution. Privacy considerations are also important: handle personally identifiable information with care and be mindful of relevant regulations. For legal defensibility, include chain-of-custody documentation in your case appendices. A practical habit is to export tool outputs and compute cryptographic hashes immediately so any future reviewer can validate that outputs have not changed. Takeaway: rigorous preservation, documentation, and cross-corroboration are as important as technical skill in forensic work. Safe Practices & Common Mistakes means always analyze copies, isolate your analysis environment, compute hashes for exports, and log every procedural step to maintain evidentiary integrity.. In practical terms, working on images, preserving chain of custody, and avoiding assumptions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Safety & Common Mistakes
Safety Checklist
  • Create verified forensic images and retain originals securely.
  • Work only on copies; keep analysis workstations isolated.
  • Record tool versions, parameters, and timestamps for every action.
  • Compute hashes for all exports and include them in appendices.
Common Mistakes
  • Assuming execution from file presence alone without corroboration.
  • Failing to validate Volatility profile, leading to poor plugin output.
  • Omitting chain-of-custody or export hashes, weakening legal defensibility.
Key practice: document everything and assume that any finding may be reviewed in court or incident reviews.

screens.title: Hands-on: Simulated Memory Dump Analysis (Conceptual)
screens.narratorSegment: This activity frames the conceptual steps you would take when given a memory dump such as memdump. raw. First, identify the Volatility profile; for a Windows 7 SP1 64-bit system, that profile is Win7SP1x64. Next, list processes using the pslist plugin to see running executables and their PIDs. Then run netscan to map network connections and relate them to processes found in pslist. If you see a suspicious process like evil. exe with PID 1234 in pslist and netscan shows PID 1234 connected to 192.0.2.50 on port 8080, that indicates the process was communicating externally and is a priority. Describe the significance: combined evidence from process listing and network connections suggests active malicious behavior rather than mere presence on disk. As a final step, export plugin outputs, compute hashes, and document each step in your report. The conceptual exercise is designed to reinforce the workflow and the importance of corroborating memory findings with disk and network artifacts before forming conclusions. pslist shows evil.exe PID 1234 and netscan shows PID 1234 connected to 192.0.2.50:8080. This pairing suggests an actively communicating malicious process; document and extract its memory region for deeper analysis.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the practical techniques investigators use after evidence is safely imaged. We begin with how to examine file systems for deleted or hidden files, read MAC timestamps, and spot executables placed in unusual locations. You will then see how the Windows Registry reveals program execution, USB history, and startup persistence. Next we explore memory forensics — how a R A M dump can show running processes, injected code, and live network sockets using the Volatility Framework. We also cover network forensics: reading PCAPs with Wireshark or tshark to find suspicious connections and data transfers. Finally, we wrap everything into a clear forensic report that answers what happened, when, how, and who, while documenting tools and chain of custody. Each technique is shown with concrete command examples and an explanation of why each artifact matters. By the end, you will understand how to extract evidence, interpret its significance, and present findings so that technical and non-technical stakeholders can act. Which artifact will you investigate first when presented with an image?

Our goals for this chapter focus on measurable forensic skills you will be able to perform. First, you'll learn to perform basic file system analysis: recovering deleted files, reading MAC timestamps, and identifying executables in unexpected locations. This skill matters because disk artifacts often show how an attacker introduced or executed tools. Second, you'll analyze Windows Registry hives to extract evidence of program execution, user activity, USB device history, and persistence mechanisms. The Registry frequently stores traces that do not appear on disk. Third, you will begin using memory forensics techniques to extract volatile evidence from R A M dumps. Memory contains live process lists, network sockets, and injected code that disk analysis cannot show. Finally in this screen you will see how to document tools and methods used, which is essential for reproducibility and legal defensibility. Each objective includes a micro-mnemonic to help you remember which artifact type contains which evidence, and a verified competency milestone indicating practical ability. Practice builds confidence: by applying these skills to preserved images and captures, you can reconstruct incidents while preserving chain of custody.

This continuation builds practical checks and mnemonics to make the forensic objectives work in live investigations. You will practice identifying deleted or hidden files and verifying their metadata to support a timeline. Next, you'll learn to parse registry hives such as NTUSER. DAT, SOFTWARE, and SYSTEM to find Run keys, RecentDocs, USB device entries, and other traces of user activity. We will also cover network capture analysis to detect C2 traffic, suspicious HTTP or DNS queries, and potential data exfiltration. Finally we emphasize safe practices: always execute analysis on forensic images, keep your analysis workstation isolated, and document every step. Each card includes why the skill matters and a small visual mnemonic to help you remember which artifact maps to which investigative question. The milestones show you what verified competency looks like in practice — for example, recovering a deleted executable and linking it to a registry Run key or an active process from a memory capture. These linkages are central to answering who, how, and when in an investigation.

File system analysis is often the first step in an investigation because it reveals persistent artifacts left on storage media. Define the scope: which file system type are you examining, NTFS or ext4, and which image represents the evidence? Start by listing directory structures and metadata to find files with unusual names, extensions, or placement. Pay attention to MAC times — modification, access, and creation timestamps — because they help sequence activity. For example, a deleted executable recovered from a temporary folder with a recent creation time but an older modification time could indicate it was copied or dropped and then executed. Use tools like Autopsy or command-line utilities to recover deleted entries if they are not yet overwritten. A common mistake is to accept a timestamp at face value without checking for time-zone shifts or system clock manipulation; corroborate with logs, registry entries, or network timestamps. Practice: run the stat command on a suspicious file to read its timestamps and compare those timestamps to related artifacts. Takeaway: file system artifacts provide durable clues, but they must be correlated with other sources to build a reliable timeline.

Recovering deleted files can produce direct evidence of attacker tools or data, but recovery has caveats. When a file is deleted, its directory entry may be removed while the underlying data blocks remain until overwritten. Forensic tools can often reconstruct these files if the sectors are intact, but success depends on subsequent disk activity. Use reputable tools like Autopsy, FTK, or EnCase to carve files from unallocated space and check file signatures against extensions. A common pitfall is relying solely on filename or extension: attackers often rename binaries or hide payloads in uncommon extensions. Another pitfall is not documenting recovery context; record offsets, hashes, and the tool used so recovered files are traceable. Also watch for cases where file timestamps do not match typical usage patterns; cross-check with registry entries for program execution, memory process lists for live evidence, and network logs for related connections. Example: you find a carved executable whose hash matches a known malware sample; confirm whether a registry Run key or a memory process with that filename existed at the same time before concluding execution. Takeaway: recovery yields candidates; corroboration yields confidence.

The Windows Registry is a hierarchical database that records configuration and activity. As an investigator, registry hives such as NTUSER. DAT, SOFTWARE, SYSTEM, and SAM contain a wealth of forensic artifacts. For example, Run keys can reveal programs configured for startup, and UserAssist entries show programs that the user executed through the GUI. Registry entries also capture recently opened documents in RecentDocs and USB device connections that help establish device history. Tools such as RegRipper parse hives into readable outputs, pulling relevant keys into a forensic timeline. When analyzing the Registry, note that timestamps are not always explicit as file MAC times are; some entries include last-write timestamps which you should interpret carefully. A good practice is to export hive data, compute hashes for extracted artifacts, and cross-correlate with disk and memory findings. One misconception is expecting the Registry to contain only configuration — it records user behavior too. The Registry often fills gaps left by deleted files because it stores persistent metadata about actions taken on the system. Windows Registry Analysis — Artifacts and hives means registry hives record system and user actions that can reveal executed programs, persistence, and device connections not visible in file listings alone.. In practical terms, extracting evidence of execution, user activity, and device history from registry hives. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Memory forensics uncovers volatile evidence that never reaches disk, such as running processes, open network sockets, injected code, and shell histories. The Volatility Framework provides plugins to list processes, scan for sockets, and detect hidden processes. When you have a memory dump and the correct profile — for example, Win7SP1x64 for a Windows 7 SP1 64-bit image — you can run pslist to enumerate processes, netscan to show network connections, psxview to compare process lists and reveal hidden ones, and cmdscan to recover command-line histories from shells. These outputs help you identify suspicious processes such as unknown executables or those with network activity. A concrete example: using pslist shows a process named evil. exe with PID 1234; netscan shows PID 1234 connected to 192.0.2.50 on port 8080. This pairing suggests active malicious communication. Remember to record the profile used, the plugin outputs, and computed hashes for any extracted dumps so your analysis is reproducible. A common misconception is assuming memory analysis is always straightforward; differences in OS versions and the need for the correct profile can affect results and require careful validation. Takeaway: memory analysis often reveals live evidence that complements disk and registry artifacts.

When you approach a memory dump, follow a reproducible process. Step one is to identify the correct Volatility profile, which matches the OS version and service pack so plugins interpret structures correctly. If you know the target is Windows 7 SP1 64-bit, use Win7SP1x64. Step two is to produce a process list with pslist to get a baseline of running programs. Step three is to run netscan to find open sockets and map them to process identifiers. If a PID appears in both outputs with suspicious network activity, flag it and run psxview to look for signs of hiding techniques. Use cmdscan to recover shell command histories that might reveal attacker commands. Throughout, export plugin output to text files and compute hashes for each exported artifact. A concrete conceptual walk-through: identify the profile as Win7SP1x64, run pslist, see evil. exe PID 1234, run netscan to confirm outward connection, then extract the memory region for that PID for deeper analysis. A common misconception is skipping profile validation; it is the single most common cause of misleading results. Volatility Walkthrough — Practical steps means identify profile, list processes, map sockets to pids, search for hidden processes, and export outputs with hashes for the report.. In practical terms, a conceptual live run: identify profile, list processes, and investigate suspicious pids. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Network forensics analyzes captured traffic to reveal communication patterns and potential exfiltration. PCAPs contain packet-level detail that helps you answer who communicated with whom and what protocols were used. Use tshark or Wireshark to apply display filters that focus on relevant traffic. Examples include filtering HTTP requests to a suspicious host or DNS queries for a malicious domain. An investigator might run a filter for HTTP traffic to a specific IP to find suspicious uploads, or filter DNS queries for a domain under investigation. Practical checks include measuring transfer sizes and timing to detect large data transfers that suggest exfiltration. Correlate network timestamps with file system and memory timestamps to see if a file was created locally just before a large upload. A common misconception is assuming encrypted channels hide all evidence; metadata such as destination IP, timing, and session sizes remain valuable. Example commands from the source show how to filter by HTTP requests and DNS queries using tshark. Takeaway: network artifacts offer visibility into attacker communication patterns and are essential for understanding the scope of compromise. In practical terms, filtering traffic, identifying suspicious hosts, and spotting exfiltration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Timeline analysis is the act of correlating timestamps and artifacts across multiple sources to build a chronological reconstruction of the incident. Start by extracting MAC times from files, last-write times from registry entries, process start times from memory captures, and packet timestamps from PCAPs. Normalize timestamps to a common reference, accounting for timezone and clock skew. Place candidate events on a timeline and look for chains of causality: a file created, a registry Run key added, a process with that filename running in memory, and a network connection soon after strongly suggests execution and external communication. The forensic report is the final product of the analysis and must communicate findings clearly and objectively. Begin with an executive summary that answers the critical questions in plain language: what happened, when, how, and who was involved as far as evidence shows. Follow with case details and scope: which drives, memory dumps, and PCAPs were examined. Document tools and methodology so others can reproduce the work, and include hashes and export filenames. Safe and defensible forensic practice begins with preserving the original evidence and working only on verified copies. Create forensic images with hashing to prove integrity, and never run analysis tools against live originals to avoid accidental modification. Maintain an isolated analysis workstation to reduce the risk of network contamination and document every action in a lab log. Common mistakes include making assumptions based on one artifact, failing to document tool versions and parameters, and forgetting to collect hashes for exported artifacts. Another frequent error is not correlating artifacts across sources, which can lead to false attribution. Privacy considerations are also important: handle personally identifiable information with care and be mindful of relevant regulations. Registry analysis extracts configuration and user activity traces from hives like NTUSER. DAT, SOFTWARE, and SYSTEM, often revealing persistence or recently run programs. Memory forensics examines R A M dumps with tools like Volatility to find running processes, active network sockets, and hidden modules. When you conduct an investigation, always correlate artifacts across disk, registry, memory, and network to increase confidence.
